name: journey

split.note: PORTRAIT ONLY, and the VERTICAL form only. At landscape a journey is one figure over a shared axis — .journey-board sets --task-count, every task carries an absolute --col, and the stage ribbon spans its tasks with grid-column: span var(--span) — so a slice leaves tasks at columns 4-5 of a grid missing columns 1-3. That is the matrix-grid/gantt test, and journey fails it at landscape: it rings there, untouched. At portrait journey.transform.js emits ol.journey-vstack > li.journey-vstage > ol.journey-vrows > li.journey-vtask and the vertical rules are flex throughout (--span is a growth factor, --col unread), so a stage is a real unit: its own band label, its own rows, a per-task mood mark rather than one polyline across the set. The categorical accent survives the cut because it is attribute-driven — .journey-vstage[data-section="0..5"] picks --cat-1-mark..--cat-6-mark — and data-section is written on the member, so it travels. The actor and mood legends FOLLOW the vstack in the emitted DOM, so they ride the suffix and repeat on every page, which a page of mood faces needs. The splitter returns null when there is no ol.journey-vstack, so the landscape grid is untouched. lib/core/carousel.js journey-stages.

renderNote: The board — stages, lanes, actors and task labels — is an HTML/CSS grid, because a journey map is fundamentally a table of text that must wrap and reflow. Drawn across it in inline `<svg>`: the mood curve and the mood faces, the only parts with real geometry. Neither side animates today — journey emits no motion roles, so chart-motion skips it.

description: Native user-journey chart — sections of tasks, each tagged with actor(s) and a 1-5 mood. Renders as section bars, task chips, plumb lines, and mood faces.
purpose: Use when a process or experience needs charting as a horizontal sequence of moments, each scored for affect. Five variants reshape the same source list: default (Mermaid-style classic), heatmap (mood-tinted chips), curve (mood polyline with axis), swimlane (per-actor rows), weighted (chip widths proportional to `+volume`).

key.description: OPTIONAL label set renaming the mood scale's two POLES: `[{1, Friction}, {5, Flow}]`, one inline-code span alone in its paragraph, outside the journey list. Only `1` and `5` are keyable — the steps between them show their number, which is the scale itself. The defaults `Pain` and `Delight` are declared in this manifest's `labelSet`; naming one pole leaves the other on its default. The rename reaches the key's accessible name too, so a screen reader and the slide cannot disagree.

heading.description: Slide heading naming the journey or process.

sections.description: Top-level li per section. Lead with the section name; nested ul carries tasks. Each task carries inline-code tokens: `@actor` (one or more), `:N` mood 1-5, optional `+N` volume (used by .weighted).

whenToUse.title: Affect is part of the story
whenToUse.body: When a process matters not just for its steps but for how each step feels. The 1-5 mood score makes the emotional contour part of the chart instead of buried in narration.

whenToUse.title: The poles are a DEFAULT, not an assertion
whenToUse.body: `Pain` and `Delight` are right for a customer journey and wrong for an ops, cost or risk one — a scale's polarity is not something the engine can derive. Write a label set outside the list — `[{1, Friction}, {5, Flow}]` — and the poles are renamed, on the slide and in the key's accessible name. Only the two poles take words; the steps between carry their number.

whenToUse.title: Actors share the trail
whenToUse.body: Use when multiple actors hand off through the sequence — customer, sales, onboarding, support. The `@actor` tokens make the handoff visible on every task chip.

whenToUse.title: One source, five lenses
whenToUse.body: Author the journey once and re-render under any variant. Heatmap for fastest scan, curve for trend, swimlane for actor load, weighted for traffic-mix — same data, different argument.

antiPatterns.title: Process without affect
antiPatterns.body: If the mood scores are all the same or arbitrary, the chart is doing less work than `timeline` or `list-steps`. Reserve journey for sequences where the affect changes meaningfully.

antiPatterns.title: More than ten tasks
antiPatterns.body: Past ten tasks the chips compress and the labels become unreadable. Group into fewer sections, or split the journey at a natural break.

antiPatterns.title: Volume tokens without weighted
antiPatterns.body: The `+N` volume token is meaningful only under the `weighted` variant. On the other four it is parsed but invisible — strip it from the markdown or commit to weighted.

commonMistakes.mistake: Keying a middle step in a label set, e.g. `[{3, Neutral}]`.
commonMistakes.fix: Only the two POLES are keyable — `1` and `5`. The steps between show their number, which IS the scale; a word on step 3 would compete with the number beside it. `lint:deck` says so, quoting the manifest's own reason.

commonMistakes.mistake: Treating the mood scale as if 1 were best instead of worst.
commonMistakes.fix: The mood scale runs 1 (worst) to 5 (best) — authoring it inverted flips heatmap tinting and the curve variant's trend direction.

commonMistakes.mistake: Assuming an omitted `:N` mood token leaves the task unplotted.
commonMistakes.fix: Omitting `:N` silently defaults the task to a neutral mood of 3 — it still plots normally under every variant, just without a deliberate score. Always give an explicit `:N` so the chart reflects real affect instead of a silent default.

variantDecisionRule.useWhen: The classic Mermaid-style read — the plainest, most familiar rendering of the sequence.
The fastest scan matters more than a precise trend — mood-tinted chips let the audience read the emotional contour at a glance.
The trend across the journey is the point — a mood polyline with an axis makes the trajectory, not just each moment, legible.
Actor load and handoff is the story — splits the journey into one row per actor.
Traffic volume through each step matters as much as mood — chip width encodes the `+N` volume token.

handles.note: An actor chip is a colored dot plus a name span, so there is no nested block to cut a header from and the whole chip becomes the handle.
A task cell is its actor initials plus a label span; the projection names the task by its label.
The portrait board's stage: a name span above a row list, so the cue that opens with the stage name had nothing to land on.
A lane header is a label span beside its span count; the cue opens with the lane's name.
